newsitem.title: USA: N.Y.C. wants control of block grant for welfare.
newsitem.headline: N.Y.C. wants control of block grant for welfare.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who hopes to build his national reputation by arguing the case for protecting immigrants' welfare benefits, on Friday said the city should get control of a block grant.

The new federal welfare reforms replace the main cash program and smaller programs with block grants, which give states more freedom in setting their own plans, though they must comply with strict new rules, like five-year time limits.

New York State in the 1998 fiscal year is expected to get a $2.4 billion block grant, and New York City, which accounts for about 66 percent of the state's welfare caseload, fears that it will not get its fair share.

"What I would like to see is for New York City to get the block grant and to administer it directly, even with some reduction," said Giuliani at a news conference on welfare held for the international press.

This would enable the city to more effectively manage its program, Giuliani said, adding he will try to persuade both the state and the federal government to soften some of the restraints imposed by the new rules.

"What we will do is to try to urge the state to make reductions that are timed over a longer period of time so that we can manage the program better and achieve savings but we don't hurt people," he explained.

Gov. George Pataki in mid-October said he plans to send a new welfare bill to the legislature over the next several weeks. He is expected to call the legislature back into session to take up the bill, probably in December.

Arguing that some targets in the new federal welfare bill are unrealistic, Giuliani said the city will press Washington to provide more funds for programs like daycare, which help parents move from collecting benefits to getting paychecks.
Welfare recipients must begin working two years after getting benefits under the new federal reforms.
However, the mayor noted that the state cannot afford to fund the programs that the federal government is cutting.
The sweeping federal welfare reforms, which were signed into law in August, would prevent most legal immigrants from getting food stamps and income for the elderly and disabled.

The city in early October sued the federal government over new welfare and immigration rules that let allow city employees turn in illegal immigrants who seek services like police protection, hospital services and public education. A 1985 New York City executive order forbids city employees from reporting illegal immigrants, except for criminal suspects.
The city also might sue the federal government on another front: whether it is fair to deny benefits to legal immigrants whose taxes support such programs.

However, the mayor, who gave no timeframe for when a second suit might be filed, noted that it needed more analysis because the city's standing is less clear. As a result, it would have to work closely with community groups, who represent legal immigrants who are directly affected.

Gov. Pataki, in a brief outline of the state's welfare bill that he submitted to Washington for its approval in mid-October, signaled that he would seek to protect Medicaid and some other benefits for legal immigrants.

New York City had about 400,000 undocumented aliens in 1993, according to court papers. Under the new federal welfare plan, an estimated 130,000 of the city's immigrants would lose their food stamps by 1998, while nearly 31,000 would be denied supplemental security income, with almost 18,500 would lose Medicaid.
